# Results — Study 892 (Corporate-Bond Ladder)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **a
held-to-maturity bond LADDER beats a constant-maturity bond FUND** (the ladder holds each
rung to par and reinvests at the new yield; the fund is "forced to sell falling bonds",
"so the ladder shines through a rate shock like 2022") — raced on liquid total-return
ETFs: a duration-staggered Treasury **ladder** (SHY/IEI/IEF/TLT) vs the **AGG**/**BND**
constant-maturity funds, with **BIL** as the cash leg. Offline & deterministic once
cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. Data is as-of 2026-06-30
(**as-of 2026-06-30** — the last complete calendar month; the partial current month is
dropped). Fingerprint `4eeca3d56739`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily **total-return** closes (`auto_adjust=True`): SHY, IEI, IEF, TLT, AGG, BND, LQD, BIL — public, no key |
| Joint window | **2007-06-30 → 2026-06-30**, **229** monthly observations (starts at BND/BIL inception — the youngest legs) |
| Ladder recipes | **EW ladder** = ¼ each SHY/IEI/IEF/TLT (blended duration **7.5y**); **duration-matched ladder** = 0.165 SHY / 0.165 IEI / 0.67 IEF (**6.0y**, tuned to AGG) |
| Fund | **AGG** (headline) and **BND**, constant-maturity one-ticker aggregate funds (duration ~6.0y / 5.9y) |
| Durations | fund fact-sheet effective durations (iShares/Vanguard, 2025), hardcoded in [`data.py`](../bond_ladder/data.py); good to ~0.3y — enough to duration-match |
| Inference | excess-of-**BIL** Sharpe with a **circular-block bootstrap** CI (block 6); **Newey-West HAC *t*** (6 lags) on the ladder-minus-fund monthly diff; three-era cut; calendar-year table |
| Costs | the ETF ladder is rolled annually (turnover × 2 × one-way spread, spread over 12 months); the one-ticker fund is buy-and-hold (free) |

> **Selection / short-history note (Signal axis).** All eight ETFs are live survivors; the
> joint window is bounded at 2007-06 by the youngest funds (BND, BIL), so the tape covers
> the GFC, ZIRP, and the 2022 shock but only ~19 years. The ladder-vs-fund gap is a
> per-month arithmetic property of two baskets, not a cross-sectional pick, so
> survivorship bias is minor — but the **structure** caveat is central (below).

> **The structure caveat, front-loaded.** For a *default-free* bond, held-to-maturity vs
> mark-to-market is an **accounting distinction, not an economic one**: the "pull to par"
> is the exact mechanical reversal of the mark-to-market loss the fund reports, so over a
> full horizon two portfolios of *equal duration* earn the *same* total return. And the
> ETF proxy is itself imperfect — SHY/IEI/IEF/TLT are *constant-maturity* funds, so a
> basket of them is another constant-maturity portfolio, **not a true HTM ladder** (a real
> ladder needs defined-maturity rungs: iBonds / BulletShares).

## Headline — duration-matched Treasury ladder vs AGG (excess-of-cash race)

| Leg | Duration | Ann return | Excess-of-BIL Sharpe | Sharpe 95% CI | Max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Duration-matched ladder | 6.0y | +3.02%/yr | 0.334 | [−0.13, +0.81] | −18.3% |
| **AGG fund** | 6.0y | **+3.07%/yr** | **0.386** | [−0.08, +0.90] | −17.1% |
| BND fund | 5.9y | +3.10%/yr | 0.396 | — | −17.3% |

**Ladder − fund = −0.01%/yr (−0.11 bps/mo), HAC *t* = −0.02** (one-sample *t* = −0.02). The
difference-Sharpe is **−0.005 with a bootstrap 95% CI of [−0.48, +0.46]** — squarely
straddling zero. Duration-matched, the Treasury ladder and the aggregate fund are a
**statistical dead heat**; if anything the fund edges it on risk-adjusted terms via its
credit/MBS diversification. There is no held-to-maturity premium to find, exactly as the
default-free accounting identity demands.

## The naive ladder that retail actually buys — it *loses*

The equal-weight SHY/IEI/IEF/TLT basket (25% long-bond TLT) carries a **7.5y** duration —
1.5y longer than AGG. That extra rate risk is *not* rewarded:

| Ladder | Duration | Ann return | Excess-of-BIL Sharpe | Max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **EW ladder** (¼ each) | 7.5y | +2.92%/yr | **0.276** | −23.2% |
| AGG fund | 6.0y | +3.07%/yr | **0.386** | −17.1% |

The naive ladder's *lower* Sharpe (0.28 vs 0.39) and *deeper* drawdown (−23% vs −17%) are
entirely a **duration bet in disguise**: it simply took more rate risk. A *shorter* ladder
(SHY/IEI/IEF, 4.6y) "wins" on Sharpe only by the same mechanism in reverse — less duration.

## Era cut — a real structural premium is stable; this one flips sign

| Era | n | Ladder ann | AGG ann | Ladder − fund | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2007-2015 | 103 | +5.10% | +4.46% | **+0.67%/yr** | +0.57 |
| 2016-2021 | 72 | +2.70% | +3.35% | **−0.60%/yr** | −0.87 |
| 2022-2026 | 54 | −0.39% | +0.12% | **−0.53%/yr** | −1.09 |

The sign **flips** across eras and never clears |*t*| ≥ 1. The 2007-2015 pure-Treasury
"win" is a **flight-to-quality / no-credit-losses** effect (AGG's credit hurt it in 2008),
not HTM; the 2016-2026 "loss" is AGG's credit spread earning its keep in calmer/rising
regimes. Every gap is a **composition** (duration + credit) story, none is structure.

## 2022 rate shock — the stress test the claim leans on

| Year | Ladder | AGG | Gap (ladder − fund) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2021 | −2.75% | −1.77% | −0.99 pp |
| **2022** | **−12.42%** | **−13.02%** | **+0.60 pp** |
| 2023 | +3.90% | +5.66% | −1.75 pp |

The duration-matched **pure-Treasury** ladder did beat AGG *in calendar 2022* — by
**+0.60 pp** — but not because it held bonds to maturity: it dodged the **credit-spread
widening** that hit AGG's corporate/MBS sleeve. And it **gave the whole thing back in
2023** (−1.75 pp) as spreads recovered. Over the full 2022-2026 hiking-and-recovery era the
ladder **trailed** AGG by −0.53%/yr. The "ladder shines through the shock" story is a
one-year credit-composition artefact, fully reversed the next year — not a durable edge.

## Tradability — costs only make it worse

The ETF ladder must be rolled/rebalanced annually across four funds; the one-ticker fund is
bought once and held. Charging the ladder (the fund pays nothing):

| Scenario | Ladder cost | Gross diff | Net diff | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 3 bp spread × 15% turnover | 0.9 bps/yr | −0.01%/yr | **−0.02%/yr** | −0.04 |
| 5 bp spread × 30% turnover | 3.0 bps/yr | −0.01%/yr | **−0.04%/yr** | −0.07 |

The friction is tiny (bond ETFs are cheap and turnover is low) — but there is **no gross
edge for it to protect**. Net, the ladder is behind. Nothing to harvest.

## Synthetic control — the machinery is faithful *(never market evidence)*

Deterministic world (`synthetic_world`, seed 892): ladder and fund share a duration factor
plus carry; the ladder additionally earns a planted premium.

| Planted premium | Recovered | HAC *t* |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 %/yr (null) | ~0 (20-seed HAC *t* mean +0.20, sd 1.36; fires 3/20) | ~0 |
| +1.5 %/yr | **+1.22 %/yr** | **+3.99** |

The estimator recovers a *planted* ladder premium at HAC *t* ≈ 4 and stays ~silent on the
null — so the real-tape **HAC *t* = −0.02** is a genuine non-result, not a dead detector.

## Verdict

- **Signal — None.** Duration-matched, the Treasury ladder minus the AGG fund is
  **−0.01%/yr at HAC *t* = −0.02**, with a difference-Sharpe bootstrap CI of [−0.48, +0.46]
  straddling zero, and the sign **flips across eras** (+0.67 / −0.60 / −0.53 %/yr, all
  |*t*| < 1.1). The naive equal-weight ladder actually **underperforms** (Sharpe 0.28 vs
  0.39) purely on extra duration. The "held-to-maturity beats the fund" premium is an
  **accounting illusion** for default-free bonds — the pull-to-par is the exact reversal of
  the fund's mark-to-market loss — and what small gaps exist are **duration + credit
  composition**, not structure. Even the 2022 "win" (+0.60 pp) is a credit-spread dodge
  fully reversed in 2023 (−1.75 pp). Short ~19-year survivor tape, named above.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** There is no gross edge to trade, and the ETF ladder pays annual
  roll/rebalance costs (0.9–3.0 bps/yr) that the one-ticker buy-and-hold fund does not, so
  net it is **strictly behind** (−0.02 to −0.04%/yr, HAC *t* ≈ 0). The ladder's appeal is
  **behavioral** (no realized-loss statements, predictable cash flows) — real comfort, but
  not a risk-adjusted return you can bank.
